### closeFingersThatMissed {#closefingersthatmissed}

Whether a finger that never meets the object closes anyway.

On, a hand holding a mug by thumb and forefinger curls its remaining fingers into the palm,
which is what a real one does. Off, they keep following the tracking, which is better for a
flat object a hand rests on rather than grips.

### easeIn {#easein}

How long the fingers take to reach the solved shape, in seconds.

The search is instant - it happens inside one frame - so without this the hand changes
shape between two frames, which reads as a glitch rather than as a hand closing.

```csharp
[Range(0, 0.5)]
public float easeIn
```

### measureFingersFromMesh {#measurefingersfrommesh}

Whether each bone is probed at its own thickness, read off the hand's mesh.

On, which is right for any hand that has a mesh. A finger stops where its skin meets the
object and the search works on bones, so the gap between the two is the finger's own
half-thickness - and that is not one number. On the hands this framework ships it runs
from 1.4 mm at a fingertip to 7.8 mm at the thumb's last joint, so one radius for all of
them leaves the thin ones hanging off the surface and the thick ones sunk into it.

```csharp
public bool measureFingersFromMesh
```

### steps {#steps}

How finely the bend is searched, as steps across the whole range.

Not the number of physics queries: the search runs coarsely first and only refines around
the step that made contact, so a hundred steps costs about thirty probes per finger rather
than a hundred.

```csharp
[Range(10, 400)]
public int steps
```

**Returns** [`int`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.int32)
